intuition: A subsequence may skip characters, so matching s against one contiguous part of t is too restrictive. Enumerating every choice of positions in t is the opposite extreme: it explores many index combinations even though most decisions can be made immediately while scanning.

The useful state is the next unmatched character of s. When t supplies that character, accept the earliest available occurrence. Waiting for a later occurrence cannot create more space for the remaining characters; it only removes potential positions from the suffix.

This gives a one-way scan with two kinds of progress: every character advances through t, but only a match advances through s. The matched counter always describes a prefix of s already found in order. Reaching the length of s proves all required characters have distinct matching positions.

The full scan makes every t position available to the visual walkthrough. A result-only variant can return true immediately for empty s or after its final required character matches; that saves work on easy inputs while preserving the same worst-case O(len(t)) bound.

steps: For s=abc and t=ahbgdc, begin with matched=0, so the next required character is a.
At t index 0, a matches s[0]; set matched=1 and now require b.
At index 1, h is unrelated to the next requirement, so leave matched unchanged.
At index 2, b matches s[1]; set matched=2 and now require c.
Characters g and d at indices 3 and 4 are skipped. At index 5, c matches and matched becomes 3.
Since matched equals len(s)=3, return true. The selected indices 0,2,5 preserve order while allowing gaps.
